summary_html: **Healthcare encounters** that reveal suspected abuse or neglect trigger reporting obligations. Federal law governs mandatory reporting in federal facilities and coordination with state systems.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — state reporter systems and protections  
- **Victims of Child Abuse Act (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — mandates in federal settings, CAC coordination

primary_citations.citation_text: California - Penal Code §§ 11164–11174.3 (CANRA – Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Act)
California - Welfare & Institutions Code § 300 et seq. (Juvenile dependency proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that the absolute immunity Penal Code section 11172(a) confers on mandated reporters barred the parents' claims against the physician and hospital arising from a report of suspected child abuse, notwithstanding the loss of any civil remedy.
key_cases.relevance: Applies the immunity directly to medical practitioners and their employers reporting suspected abuse discovered in treatment.
key_cases.quote: The Legislature's solution in bestowing absolute immunity to the enumerated professionals was an attempt to remove one of the largest impediments to reporting

key_cases.holding: The court reversed a dismissal and held that a child states a cause of action against a physician and hospital for negligently failing to diagnose battered child syndrome and to report it as Penal Code section 11161 then required, because both the standard of care and proximate cause are questions of fact.
key_cases.relevance: Directly governs a physician's obligation in a healthcare encounter to recognize and report the injuries that signal abuse.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, the trial court in the case at bar could not properly rule as a matter of law that the defendants' negligence was not the proximate cause of plaintiff's injuries.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed jurisdictional and dispositional orders entered after a mother who asked her physician for help with cocaine use was referred to the agency, holding the juvenile court did not abuse its discretion in declaring the child a dependent rather than ordering family maintenance services under section 360(b).
key_cases.relevance: Illustrates the physician's referral of a family to the agency based on a patient's disclosure during treatment.
key_cases.quote: The court has broad discretion to determine what would best serve and protect the child's interest and to fashion a dispositional order in accord with this discretion.

Written risk assessment no later than 30 days, and before the referral is closed or promoted to a case
